Examine SECO's specific penalty thresholds for Swiss commodity traders caught breaching secondary Iran sanctions. (1)

In Switzerland, the enforcement of international trade restrictions and asset freezes is legally governed by the Federal Act on the Implementation of International Sanctions (Embargo Act, EmbA). Under this statutory framework, the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) operates as the primary investigating, prosecuting, and adjudicating authority for sanctions infractions. 

https://t.co/2DKbQDM2ly

For Swiss-registered commodity traders navigating complex energy and maritime networks, SECO applies distinct criminal penalty thresholds based on the intent, negligence, and structural severity of the violation:

https://t.co/MFTBKG8VN4

1. Statutory Criminal Penalty Thresholds under the EmbA

Swiss law does not utilize a separate civil penalty regime for trade violations; all sanctions breaches are treated as administrative criminal offenses governed by the Federal Act on Administrative Criminal Law (ACL):

https://t.co/2DKbQDM2ly

•Intentional (Wilful) Violations (Art. 9, Para. 1): If a commodity trading desk knowingly bypasses restrictions—such as fabricating end-user certificates or utilizing illicit maritime routes to facilitate barred trades—individuals can face up to 1 year of imprisonment or a substantial monetary penalty.

https://t.co/IUmO0ZHlU2

•Serious and Aggravated Cases (Art. 9, Para. 2): For major corporate infractions, structural evasion, or repetitive illicit trade operations, the penalty threshold escalates significantly to up to 5 years of custodial imprisonment combined with statutory fines of up to CHF 1 million. 

https://t.co/w44hl0IM8c

•Negligent Breaches (Art. 9, Para. 3): If a firm fails to properly audit its supply chains or verify a third-party intermediary, resulting in an inadvertent breach, the infraction is penalized with a fine of up to CHF 100,000. 

https://t.co/IUmO0ZHlU2

2. Violations of Information and Disclosure Requests (Art. 10)

During an active investigation or routine audit of a Geneva- or Zug-based trading desk, SECO holds the legal power to demand internal shipping manifests, bank clearing receipts, and communications: 

https://t.co/IUmO0ZHlU2

•Wilful Refusal or False Statements: Intentionally providing falsified trade data, masking beneficial owners, or refusing to cooperate with a SECO disclosure order carries a fine threshold of up to CHF 100,000. 

https://t.co/w44hl0IM8c

•Negligent Reporting Omissions: Inadvertently submitting incomplete compliance documentation or missing mandatory declaration windows is punishable by a fine of up to CHF 40,000. 

https://t.co/w44hl0IM8c

3. Corporate Liability and the "Disproportionate Investigation" Rule

In routine corporate enforcement, SECO frequently relies on specific procedural efficiencies permitted under the Administrative Criminal Law (ACLA): 

https://t.co/MFTBKG8VN4

•The CHF 5,000 Threshold (Art. 7, Para. 1 ACLA): If identifying and prosecuting the specific individual executive responsible within a complex corporate hierarchy would require an excessively long, expensive, or disproportionate investigation, SECO is legally authorized to drop individual prosecution. Instead, the agency shifts liability directly to the legal corporate entity, issuing a streamlined penalty order capped at CHF 5,000 or less, plus substantial procedural and audit costs.

Exemption from Liability of Intermediaries in Certain Cases

Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides legal protection to intermediaries against liability for third-party content hosted or transmitted through their platforms.

An intermediary includes social media platforms, internet service providers, web-hosting companies, search engines, and similar online service providers. Examples include X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube.

Sub-section (1)

An intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, subject to the conditions specified in the Act.

Sub-section (2)

This protection applies only if:

The intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system through which information is transmitted, temporarily stored, or hosted;

The intermediary does not initiate the transmission;

The intermediary does not select the receiver of the transmission;

The intermediary does not select or modify the information contained in the transmission; and

The intermediary observes due diligence and complies with the requirements prescribed under the Act and the applicable rules.

Sub-section (3)

The protection under Section 79 shall not apply if:

1. The intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided, or induced the commission of an unlawful act; or

2. Upon receiving actual knowledge, or upon being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency that any information, data, or communication link hosted on its computer resource is being used to commit an unlawful act, the intermediary fails to expeditiously remove or disable access to such material while preserving evidence.

Explanation

The term “Third Party Information” refers to any information dealt with by an intermediary in its capacity as an intermediary.

Practical Significance

Section 79 provides a “safe Harbour” to intermediaries. As a result, social media platforms and other intermediaries are generally not automatically liable for content posted by their users. However, if they participate in unlawful activities or fail to act after receiving a valid legal notice or government direction, they may lose the protection granted under Section 79.

The scope of this provision was further clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Court held that “Actual knowledge” for the purposes of Section 79 generally arises through a court order or a notification issued by a competent government authority, requiring the intermediary to take appropriate action.

Today is Election Day in the United States.

And a federal court has issued a ruling involving the use of government identity information.

US District Judge Tanya Chutkan temporarily barred the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security from sending states lists of voters suspected of being noncitizens or urging officials to segregate or withhold their ballots based on those lists.

The ruling concerns the reliability of the information and the government's authority to use it.

The administration argues that the effort is intended to enforce the federal prohibition on noncitizen voting.

Voting rights and privacy organizations argue that the process risks incorrectly identifying eligible voters and violates privacy protections.

The judge expressed concern that unreliable data could disenfranchise legitimate voters.

The order is temporary.

It doesn't establish that every government record is incorrect.

And it doesn't eliminate the legal requirement that voters meet applicable eligibility rules.

But it raises a question that extends far beyond elections.

What happens when an organization treats a database match as proof of someone's identity or legal status?

Consider two records.

One contains a person's name and date of birth.

Another contains similar information.

A matching system determines that the records probably refer to the same person.

That can be useful.

But the match itself may be incorrect.

People share names.

Records contain outdated information.

Dates can be entered incorrectly.

And an individual's status may change after a record was created.

A system that produces a probable match doesn't necessarily establish a current legal fact.

That distinction becomes particularly important when the result affects someone's rights.

In financial services, an incorrect identity match can prevent someone from opening an account.

In employment, it can cause a background check to associate someone with another person's records.

In healthcare, it can contribute to mistakes involving patient information.

And in elections, it can affect whether an eligible voter is permitted to cast a ballot that counts.

The consequences depend on the application.

But the underlying data problem is similar.

An organization needs to understand what its records establish and how reliable they are.

It also needs a process for correcting errors.

That process matters because people may have little control over the information stored about them.

They may not know which databases were consulted.

They may not know why a match occurred.

And they may not have an easy way to challenge the result.

The government's interest in enforcing election eligibility requirements is legitimate.

So is the public's interest in ensuring that eligible voters aren't incorrectly excluded.

Those objectives require accurate information and appropriate procedures.

I think identity systems should be evaluated according to the consequences of incorrect decisions.

A false match in a low-risk application might be inconvenient.

A false match that affects someone's legal rights demands stronger safeguards.

That includes reliable source data, documented decision rules, and meaningful opportunities to correct mistakes.

A database match is evidence to evaluate. Its reliability needs to be established before it becomes the basis for a consequential decision.

SCOPE: Target = that single parent post. Images, charts, screenshots, or video frames that are NATIVE to the target post are in scope — read them and check the claims they make. Quoted or embedded content from other accounts is context only. If an image isn't legible enough to verify a claim, treat that as low confidence → NO (unprovable). If the target contains no checkable factual claim of its own, reply exactly: NO (no claim).

STEP 1 — EXTRACT: Identify the single most specific, central factual claim the target asserts OR clearly presupposes — in its text or its image — even when it's embedded in a question, prediction, conditional, sarcasm, or insult. Leading questions often smuggle in a claim: e.g. "more stolen elections" presupposes elections were already stolen; "why did they hide the evidence?" presupposes evidence was hidden; "if X, that proves a crime" asserts a standard of proof. State the claim verbatim or as a precise one-sentence paraphrase before judging it, then check it against credible sources.
- Do not substitute a broader, easier, or side claim if the central claim is harder to verify — rule on the central claim itself, even if it takes more work.
- If multiple checkable claims exist, pick the one whose falsity would most change a reader's understanding. (Choose only among genuinely checkable claims — do not pick an impactful but unfalsifiable one to flag.)

STEP 2 — OUTPUT IN THIS EXACT ORDER:

1) VERDICT (one line only):
- FALSE — the specific claim is verifiably false.
- MISLEADING — literally true but distorts via cherry-picking, omission, or false presupposition. (NOT merely "framing I dislike" — see motive rule.)
- NO (no false claim) — the claim is checkable and holds up.
- NO (unprovable) — value judgment, a prediction whose presuppositions are TRUE, an unprovable motive, or genuinely insufficient/conflicting evidence.

2) If FALSE or MISLEADING, give a NOTE DRAFT (≤450 characters):
[Neutral correction + key context, stating only what a source supports. Name no one. No snark.]
Source: [best URL]
Then on new lines add:
To add context: open the ••• menu on the post → "Request Community Note" → paste the correction + source into the "why this needs a note" box. Enough requests alert top contributors, who can publish a note.
Contributors can instead choose "Write a Community Note" and submit the draft above.

3) EXPLANATION:
- Restate the extracted claim.
- Explain why the verdict applies, with direct evidence.
- List sources with links; prefer multiple. Be transparent about confidence.

RULES (strict):
- Don't fact-check opinions, hyperbole, jokes, satire, or predictions UNLESS they rest on a clear false factual presupposition.
- Politically contested ≠ factually false. A claim settled by evidence does not become "arguable" because it's divisive.
- MOTIVE RULE: True facts + an unprovable motive or intent (why it happened, who benefits, whether it was deliberate) = NO (unprovable). "False implication" requires a false FACTUAL state of affairs, not merely bad faith or framing you distrust.
- If confidence is not high (conflicting reliable sources, ambiguous data, illegible image), default to NO (unprovable).
- Prioritize primary sources, official data, peer-reviewed studies, or fact-checkers with transparent methodology. Use tools (search, image analysis) as needed.

text:
Timepass talk on a Diwali!

1. Between the Lines: Signals from the Concall Room 

Divi's Laboratories: "...with the futuristic capacity, we will be in the top 3 players [in Peptides SPPS]..."

KSH International: "...EBITDA per tonne of approximately ₹85,000 per tonne should be sustainable..."

Azad Engineering: "...All 6 customer-dedicated facilities are now commissioned— 44,800 square meters for 4 global OEMs namely Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, GE, Vanova, Siemens Energy, and Baker Hughes.

Sigma Advanced Systems: "...the fundraise is primarily to fuel our growth coming in from M&A, right, new acquisitions. We've been working on multiple opportunities over the last 6 to 8 months, and I think next quarter, Q4, is when we expect to close these transactions..."

VA Tech Wabag: "...Our order book has surpassed ₹20,000 crores, while our net cash position has surpassed ₹1,000 crores, achieving record levels in both parameters. 

Aditya Infotech: "...In the 12 months to September 2026, our share of the total market including the unorganized segment was about 42%, which at the time of our IPO was 30%...In October, we repaid all our borrowings, and now the company is debt-free..."

Sansera Engineering: "...I'm happy to say we have already won in this quarter our first business from Safran...in the semiconductor business, we are making good progress towards adding the customer number 2..."

2. Timex Group India - Shared on June 7th, see below for the latest update

Financial Year 2025-26 marked a structural turning point for Timex Group, ending as a milestone year that fundamentally transformed the company's scale and profitability profile. Total revenue surged 48% year-on-year to ₹800 crore.

The growth was driven by a decisive shift toward premiumization. The core Timex brand expanded 62%, fashion powerhouse Guess grew 51%, and luxury anchor Versace delivered 48% growth. At the same time, e-commerce and quick commerce channels recorded a phenomenal 90% increase, highlighting the strength of the company's omnichannel strategy.

More importantly, profitability significantly outpaced revenue growth as operating leverage began to play out.

What makes this performance particularly noteworthy is that it was not driven by a single exceptional quarter. Revenue growth remained consistently strong throughout the year, with Q1 growing 55% YoY, Q2 40%, Q3 26%, and Q4 an impressive 74% YoY.

The company's sales strategy appears to be creating a sustainable high-growth trajectory. Historically, Q2 has been the strongest quarter due to festive-season bookings, while the remaining quarters were relatively subdued. This year, however, Q4 revenue reached almost 96% of Q2 levels, indicating a far more balanced and resilient demand profile across the year.

What to Expect in FY27 and FY28?

Management is positioning the company to enter the ₹1,100-1200-crore revenue club, targeting a base-case growth rate of 35-40%. This expansion will be supported by a significant increase in local manufacturing capacity, which is expected to rise from 6 million units to 10 million units annually.

While the company continues to prioritize growth, EBITDA margins are expected to stabilize in the 15–16% range. Additionally, employee expenses and administrative overheads appear to have largely normalized, creating the potential for substantial operating leverage as revenues continue to scale.

Latest update (post Q2FY27):

Posted highest-ever quarterly revenue of ₹359 crores. E-commerce grew 75% in Q2, led by Flipkart, Myntra, Amazon, 3P and quick commerce.

The Baddi plant is operating at 100% capacity (6 million units/year) and ran double shifts to meet demand. Investing $1.2 million to double the Baddi plant's capacity to 12 million units by May of next year.

In the ₹2,000–10,000 segment, the competitive landscape is largely a duopoly between Titan and Timex. While Titan's core brand business is still nearly 4x the size of Timex, management sees significant headroom to capture market share and scale up.

The company sees a potential to reach an EBITDA margin of ~20% in the future through operating leverage.

Last but not least, festive season shopping fell in Q2 last year, whereas this year it has shifted to Q3. Hence, do expect some fireworks in Q3FY27!

3. Navin Fluorine

How they make money:

Navin earns its revenue from three verticals. The business operates across i) High Performance Products (refrigerants and inorganic fluorides) - 51%, ii) Specialty Chemicals (agrochemical and industrial intermediates) - 30%, and iii) CDMO (pharma synthesis) with emerging Advanced Materials - 19%.

HPP (High Performance Products) is the biggest and covers refrigerant gases (HFCs, R32 coming), AHF/HF sold to merchant and high-purity buyers, and the HFO supply contract with Solstice Advanced Materials (the old Honeywell/Orchid business), which is a pass-through-priced, long-tenure contract on a dedicated asset.

Specialty Chemicals is mostly agrochemical and fluorination intermediates made in the multi-purpose plants (MPP-1/MPP-2) at Dahej on a campaign basis. It is running at roughly a ₹350 cr per quarter run rate, and the Nectar/Chemours project is being added.

CDMO is largely Fermion/darolutamide, made in dedicated cGMP plants, with a USD100M target for FY27 and a pipeline of other molecules behind it. Advanced Materials (data centres, semiconductors, defence, the DRDO/TDF project) is being incubated as a fourth vertical, expected to be 10-15% of the pie by 2030.

What’s working well:

Q2 revenue was ₹1,191 cr (+57% YoY), EBITDA ₹407 cr (+66%) at a 34.2% margin, and PAT ₹269 cr (+81%). H1 PAT of ₹513 cr already gives an EPS of ₹100. All three segments grew sequentially.

HPP benefited from better refrigerant gas placement than the market average, the AHF plant ramping, and higher HFO volumes.

Specialty gained from squeezing more campaigns out of existing MPP plants, and CDMO from the Fermion base plus new qualification campaigns. Gross profit held despite input inflation because forex tailwinds, pricing actions, operating leverage and efficiency gains offset sourcing costs. Working capital is at 72 days, capex is funded comfortably (H1 capex was about ₹300 cr), and the Solstice HFO contract was extended from 7 to 11 years (to December 2032) with about USD180M of added revenue potential. This protects the base beyond FY28, though the implied ~USD45M/yr run rate versus the earlier ~USD58M drew few "ouch" comments. Management says the pass-through pricing makes simple averaging misleading and that volumes are guaranteed higher.

What to expect for the rest of FY27 and FY28:

Management guided FY27 margins to stay in the H1 range (~34%), while keeping the long-term 30% EBITDA guidance unchanged. Q3 and Q4 should add several visible steps. The MPP debottlenecking (commissioned end-September) is not yet in the numbers, and R32 should give incremental revenue in Q3 with a full ramp in Q4. The Chemours project is due in Q3 with orders already in hand, and cGMP-4 Phase 2 (~₹125 cr) should start by the end of Q4.

Specialty should reach about 60-65% of Nectar’s peak annual revenue in FY27, with the rest in FY28, and CDMO should reach the USD100M order-book target. FY27 capex is guided at about ₹700 cr, at the low end of the ₹700-1,000 cr annual frame. Management says FY28 growth is “pretty much baked in” from the capex already in place, so expect continued 20-25% type growth, with cGMP-4 (₹900-1,000 cr peak potential, split across Phase 1 and Phase 2) mostly a FY28-FY29 story.

Advanced Materials adoption capacity arrives by Q2 FY28. The main swing factors are geopolitics and input costs (fluorspar, sulphur and gas are all rising), the pace of AHF utilisation, how much of the current refrigerant pricing proves durable, and whether Chemours adoption (a ~15-month read after commissioning) justifies the larger scale-up.

4. Innomet Advanced

How they make money

Innomet is a Hyderabad-based maker of engineered metal products with two divisions.

i) Metal powders (about ₹38 cr in H1, roughly 68% of revenue) are specialty powders sold by weight to parts makers, additive manufacturing and surface-coating customers. Almost 100% of this is water-atomised, and gas-atomised spherical powder has only just started with a 50 kg unit. Realisation rose from ₹959 to ₹1,487/kg.

ii) Tungsten heavy alloys (THA) (₹17.6 cr, about a third of revenue) are dense, high-value parts and fragments for defence (Pinaka, Astra), aerospace (AS9100D-certified) and other niche uses, sold per piece or per kg (₹25,000-35,000/kg indicated), with about 87% exported. Tungsten feedstock is now partly captured through the 57.5% acquisition of Swastik Tungsten, which was consolidated only for the last few days of H1. Exports were 46% of H1 revenue, against 15% a year ago. Management gave segment EBITDA margins of about 12% for powders and about 22% for THA, which blend to the reported ~15%.

What’s working well

H1 revenue more than doubled to ₹55.7 cr (from ₹23.5 cr), already above all of FY26. EBITDA was ₹8.24 cr at a 14.8% margin, up from 4.4% in H2 FY26 when tungsten prices squeezed profits, though still below 18% a year ago. PAT was ₹4.75 cr and EPS ₹3.64. Powder volumes rose 39% with 55% higher realisation, and 18 new customers were added (including Oerlikon and Medicoat). THA grew about sixfold and its mix rose from 14% to a third, which should lift margins as it grows. Exports rose about sevenfold, helped by China-plus-one sourcing, defence restocking and aerospace certification, and powder sales to the US continue despite the 50% tariff. The tungsten supply problem is described as solved by Swastik, with sourcing vendors up from 2-3 to over 60. Pricing discipline has improved (buying only against confirmed orders, shorter quote validity), and the balance sheet looks fine, with debt-to-equity at 0.36x, net worth up to ₹55 cr, and ₹37.5 cr of preferential funding (about ₹14 cr received).

What to expect for the rest of FY27 and FY28

With ₹55.7 cr delivered and ₹36.7 cr of orders in hand, FY27 revenue should clear the ₹100 cr target, and management says H2 will be “much better” than H1 if all goes well. Tungsten prices have stabilised after a sharp rise, so deferred customer orders (Indian defence programmes and Israeli buyers still in test mode) may start flowing.

Powder capacity rises from 620 to 800 tpa this year, then to 1,350 tpa in FY28 and about 1,600 tpa with the DRDO-backed atomiser.

THA’s current output is about 60 tpa (2-2.5 tonnes a month), and the 120 tpa expansion could support about ₹150 cr of revenue at current prices. Management guides FY28 growth of 30-50% (35-50% for the next two to three years) with better margins, and a long-term EBITDA margin of 16-20%. Their view is that existing assets can reach ₹400-500 cr, while the ₹1,000 cr vision depends on a new greenfield project and fresh fundraising that is “not even on the drawing board”. Swastik’s bottom line won’t improve until it moves up to carbide and pure-tungsten products, at least six months away. Tungsten hexafluoride for semiconductors is a “moonshot”, and the spark plasma sintering furnace and the EIGA atomiser for reactive powders (titanium, zirconium) are early-stage.

But if the company has to achieve ₹1,000 Cr in revenue, Tungsten Carbide is perhaps the most realistic growth avenue to get there!

5. Indo Count Industries

How they make money

Indo Count is a bed-linen and home-textile maker that sells to large retailers, mainly in the US. It runs in two segments.

The core business is bed linen made in India (sheets, duvet covers and similar), with a FY27 revenue target of about ₹4,000 cr and EBITDA margins of roughly 15% or better. Core revenue is about 70% US and about 30% non-US.

The new businesses have a FY27 target of about ₹1,500 cr. They are split roughly two-thirds utility bedding and one-third branded. Utility bedding (quilts, comforters, blankets and similar) is made in three US facilities. The branded side is built around Wamsutta, a US brand the company acquired, plus licensed brands such as Tommy Hilfiger. Revenue comes from product sales: volumes in million meters multiplied by realisation, plus the margin from branded and utility products. 

Management said gross margin should be viewed on an annual basis and should stay in a 50–55% range. Cotton is the main input cost. The company holds 4–5 months of inventory as a cushion and passes cost increases on to customers with a lag of one to two quarters. Most sales are on FOB or CIF terms, so freight increases are borne by the customer.

What’s working well

Execution is strong across the business. Q2 total income was ₹1,699 cr (+57% YoY, +39% QoQ), and EBITDA more than doubled to ₹259 cr at a 15.3% margin, against a full-year guidance of 13%. H1 revenue of ₹2,923 cr is about 52% of the full-year target, and H1 EBITDA margin is 14.4%. Management attributed the growth to market-share and wallet-share gains. Core margins are above 15%. The new businesses have reached about 30% of revenue, with Q2 revenue of about ₹502 cr and about 60% of the FY27 target already done. The three US utility plants are running above 65% utilisation. Wamsutta’s move into US retail, beyond direct-to-consumer, is a big driver on the branded side. 

The balance sheet is at its best: net debt is ₹518 cr (0.2x equity, the lowest ever), cash is ₹315 cr, annualised ROCE is 21.4% and ROE is 15.3%. Management also said working-capital days are down by at least three weeks since March, and the pass-through mechanism has protected margins so far.

Two caveats: Q2 gross margin fell, and management put that down to product mix. The new businesses’ EBITDA margin is still only “lower double digit”.

What to expect for rest of FY27 and FY28

For FY27, management said it will exceed the ₹5,500 cr revenue guidance and the 13% EBITDA margin guidance. Volume guidance is 105–110 million meters, with 51 million done in H1. The margin could reach 14–15% for the year, but management said it will not go beyond that. Rough arithmetic from the H1 run-rate suggests revenue of about ₹6,000 cr or more, though management gave no number. The new businesses’ margins should rise from lower double digits toward the core’s 15% over the next two to three quarters as the US plants fill up. The ₹250 cr capex is spread over 12–18 months, with only about ₹40 cr spent in H1. Most of the spinning capex should land in FY27, and the effluent treatment plant will probably spill into FY28. For FY28, the stated goal is ₹8,000 cr of revenue by CY28 (double the FY25 base of ₹4,000 cr), and management said this needs no growth capex. Utility plants should reach full utilisation and the branded business should reach about $100 mn, both by CY28.

The UK FTA took effect in July and the EU deal is still pending, and non-US revenue should grow by more than 20% in FY27. Management will give FY28 guidance next year. Net debt should keep falling as free cash flow comes in.

That's all for this edition. Wishing you a Sunday filled with festive sparkle, glowing diyas and plenty of Diwali cheer!

Statement: Legal notice to the Delhi Police and X Corp. over takedown demands against IFF’s account

On 3 November 2026, X Corp. forwarded to us two “Illegal Content Reports” submitted in the name of the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), @delhipolice. The first, dated 31 October, sought removal of a post we published on 30 October and a post by @SFLCin. The second, dated 2 November, sought removal of 37 posts and the withholding of three accounts in their entirety,  @internetfreedom, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia, on the ground that they defame the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. The posts in question reproduce and comment on a legal notice that was sent to us. They are protected speech under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. We were given no notice before these reports were filed. We learnt of them only because X forwarded copies.

Today, through our counsel Advocate Abhik Chimni and his colleagues, we served a legal notice on the Delhi Police, with a copy to X Corp.

Our position is simple:

1. Defamation is a non-cognizable offence. The police cannot investigate it without a Magistrate’s order, and cognizance can be taken only on a complaint by the person aggrieved.

2. The reports cite no complaint, no FIR, no Magistrate’s order and no court order, even though the box for “enforcement of court order” was ticked. Under Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, an intermediary can be required to take down content only on a court order or a reasoned government notification. A web form with “hate speech”, “defamation”, “safety/security” and “court order” ticked against 40 URLs, with one sentence of reasons, is not that.

3. Whether something is defamatory is for a court to decide after hearing the author. A police officer cannot decide it himself and direct a platform to act on his decision. Demanding that three accounts be withheld in full is grossly disproportionate to any grievance stated.

We have called upon the Delhi Police to withdraw both reports or disclaim within seven days, to furnish us the complaint and authority on which they were made, and to confirm that no further takedown requests will be made on this matter. If they do not, we will approach the Delhi High Court under Article 226. We have also requested X Corp. to take no action on the reports pending their withdrawal or adjudication. 

We are grateful to Advocate Abhik Chimni and his team for representing us in this matter. Redacted copies of the notice are attached.

Delhi Police asks X to take down IFF's account and posts. IFF will challenge the notices in court unless they are withdrawn.

The Delhi Police has asked X to remove the Internet Freedom Foundation's account, six of its posts, the accounts of SFLC and @geoblockedindia, and posts by 16 other users, on the ground that they defame the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh. The posts document and comment on a legal notice sent in the RSS's name to IFF, SFLC and @geoblockedindia, which demanded that the three stop criticising and documenting government blocking orders. IFF received copies of the two police notices from X on the morning of 3 November 2026.
IFF calls on the Delhi Police to withdraw both notices. If they are not withdrawn, IFF will challenge them in court.

What has happened

On 29 October 2026 at 9:54 PM, IFF, SFLC and the operator of @geoblockedindia received a two-page "legal notice" said to be issued on behalf of the RSS. It asked the three to stop opposing the government's blocking directions, stop documenting restricted content, stop posting details of geo-blocked posts, and confirm in writing within seven days that they would comply. It was signed by an unnamed "Authorised Signatory". Several RSS office-bearers have since said on X that the notice is not authentic. IFF replied to the notice, wrote to the RSS at its official address asking whether it had authorised it, and published both the notice and its reply on 30 October.

On 31 October 2026 at 8:06 PM, the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), Delhi Police, filed an "Illegal Content Report" with X (reference LD-321926). It listed two posts: IFF's post of 30 October on the notice, and SFLC post of the same day. The stated reason was that the posts are "defamatory towards the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023". The boxes for "safety/security", "defamation" and "other" were ticked. The fields for the nature of the court order and court order details were left empty. The desired action was "Remove/withhold content".

On 1 November 2026, a second notice arrived in the RSS's name. It said the matter had been handed to the Akhil Bharatiya Adhivakta Parishad, that complaints had been filed in several states, and that requests had been made to block IFF's X account and suspend the organisations. The Delhi Police had made its first request to X the previous evening. IFF did not know this until X told it on 3 November.

On 2 November 2026 at 8:51 AM, the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) filed a second notice with X (reference LD-322956). It lists 40 URLs. Thirty-seven are posts. Three are the entire accounts of @internetfreedom, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia. This time the boxes for "Hate speech", "defamation", "safety/security", "enforcement of court order" and "other" were all ticked. The court order fields were again left empty. The stated reason reads: "The posts constitute defamation and illegal content under Section 356 BNS. Under Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, read with Section 79(3)(b) IT Act, lawful notices require action within 3 hours."

The 16 other users are @ProdctiveUseful, @PanjwaniManoj, @jidge_, @RatanSharda55, @baxiabhishek, @SchrdingersDbag, @ashleshbiradar, @seemay, @NasirHussainINC, @Being_creat_ive, @AjoyDharmavaram, @othlaw, @_ananyaaa, @AimPoojaind, @incorigibleBhai and @rraoind. Their posts, as far as IFF can tell, comment on the notice or on the notice about it.

X forwarded both notice to IFF on 3 November 2026, at 8:47 AM and 10:03 AM, saying it was doing so "in the interest of transparency" and that IFF may wish to seek legal counsel and challenge the request in court. X's emails do not say that it has acted on the requests. The Delhi Police has not written to IFF, and no court has been approached, as far as the reports disclose. SFLC and @geoblockedindia have separately reported notifications from X about requests from the Uttar Pradesh Police, the Telangana Police and the Delhi Police's Cyber Crime unit, one of them against the whole of the @geoblockedindia account.

IFF's position

IFF condemns this legal action. A police force has made itself the enforcement arm of a private legal notice whose authenticity the organisation it names has not confirmed, and whose demand was that three organisations stop documenting censorship. The notices would deliver exactly what the notice asked for as they would also remove the accounts of the three groups in India that keep public records of what is blocked, and of who ordered it.

The posts in question are about a legal notice sent to us. They quote it, criticise how it was drafted, and say that we will carry on with our work. A person who receives a threat is entitled to publish it and answer it and that is not defamation of the sender. 

In the three weeks before the first notice, IFF assisted 86 people whose accounts were suspended or whose posts were withheld in India. SFLC's Free Speech Tracker recorded about 268 content restrictions and 83 account restrictions in the first 29 days of October. @geoblockedindia publishes the orders behind such blocks when platforms disclose them. None of this is unlawful. Documenting censorship and challenging it in court is what the Constitution expects of citizens.
IFF will not delete the posts. If the Delhi Police does not withdraw the notices, we will challenge them in court.

Why the reports are unlawful

Defamation is not a police matter. Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is a non-cognizable and bailable offence. Under Section 222 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, no court can take cognizance of it except on a complaint by the person aggrieved. 

Under Section 174 of the BNSS, the police cannot investigate a non-cognizable offence without an order of a Magistrate. The Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) is not the person aggrieved. The notices disclose no complaint by the RSS and no order of any Magistrate. Whether a statement is defamatory is for a court to decide after hearing its author, with the defences of truth, fair comment and good faith available to that author. 

In Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India, (2016) 7 SCC 221, the Supreme Court upheld criminal defamation on the strength of these safeguards. A police officer who asks a platform to remove speech as defamatory has decided the question himself, without a complainant, a court or a hearing.

The posts are protected comment. Exceptions 1 to 3 to Section 356(1) protect the truth published for the public good, opinion on the public conduct of public servants, and opinion on the conduct of any person touching a public question. The posts publish a notice that was sent to us and give our opinion of it. The RSS, if it sent the notice, chose to enter a public question. If it did not, the posts defame no one.

Further, Section 79(3)(b) and Rule 3(1)(d) do not permit this. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down Section 79(3)(b) so that an intermediary acquires "actual knowledge" only through a court order, or a notification from the appropriate government or its agency that unlawful acts relatable to Article 19(2) are being committed. The court said that it would be difficult for intermediaries to judge the legitimacy of the millions of requests they receive, and that the burden must not be placed on them. Rule 3(1)(d), as amended in November 2025 and February 2026, now requires the intimation to come from an officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary or Deputy Inspector General, to be reasoned, and to specify the legal basis and the nature of the unlawful act, subject to a monthly review by a Secretary-level officer. The three-hour window the notice invokes applies to a lawful order that meets these conditions. A web form that ticks "hate speech" and "enforcement of court order" while leaving the court order fields blank, and that gives one sentence of reasons for 40 URLs, is not such an order.

The notices by the Delhi Police are disproportionate. They seek to remove three accounts in their entirety, with years of posts, over six, four and eleven posts respectively. They sweep in 16 third parties whose only connection is that they commented on a public controversy. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that any restriction on speech must be necessary, proportionate and the least restrictive measure available, and that orders restricting speech must be published and reasoned. Removing an organisation's entire account for criticising a legal notice fails each of these tests.

The effect is to silence documentation of censorship and providing legal aid to Indian internet users. The accounts named are those that record blocking orders in India. The notice asked them to stop. A takedown request that accomplishes the demand of an anonymous private notice is not law enforcement. It is the use of state power for a private end, which Article 14 forbids.

Our demands

1. To the Delhi Police: Withdraw reports LD-321926 and LD-322956 and confirm the withdrawal in writing to X and to IFF. 

2. To the Delhi Police: Disclose the complaint on which the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) acted, the authority under which the reports were filed, and whether any order of a Magistrate under Section 174 BNSS exists. Disclose every request made to any platform in this matter, including those made by the Cyber Crime unit against @geoblockedindia.

3. To X: Do not act on the reports. If any content is withheld in India, tell the affected user before acting, give them the full request, and name the legal basis. Publish both reports to the Lumen database, as the reporting form itself contemplates.

4. To the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology and the Ministry of Home Affairs: Have the Secretary-level review required by Rule 3(1)(d) examine these intimations, and tell police forces that Rule 3(1)(d) is not a remedy for defamation, which the law reserves to the person aggrieved and to the courts.

5. To the RSS: State publicly whether it authorised either notice or any complaint to the police. If it did not, say so to the Delhi Police.

If the notices are not withdrawn, IFF will challenge them in court. We will continue to document blocking orders, to publish them, and to provide legal assistance to anyone whose account or post is withheld in India. Nothing in these notices changes that.

Analysis| India’s War on Truth

Following an unexpected and heavy military setback against Pakistan in the early phase of the recent Indo-Pak conflict, the Indian government launched a coordinated effort to silence international media and local voices that reported these losses—dismissing it all as a Pakistan-backed disinformation campaign.

🔻Weaponizing Censorship:

Over 8,000 social media accounts were blocked, including those of BBC Urdu, The Wire, Maktoob Media, and almost all Pakistani news channels.

Independent journalists like Anuradha Bhasin and Muzamil Jaleel had their accounts suspended under vague charges of treason. 
16 youtube accounts belonging to various Pakistani podcasters and media outlets were blocked.

Platforms like X (formerly Twitter) were threatened with steep fines and arrests of local staff if they refused to comply. 
X stated that many government takedown orders, lacked proper justification or legal basis.

🔻Rise of Propaganda & State-Driven Nationalism:

Pro-government outlets pushed dramatic, unverified claims such as “Karachi Port destroyed” and “26 cities wiped out”

Figures like retired Major Gaurav Arya publicly called for "burning Pakistani cities" —critics say this reflects state-enabled jingoism.

International journalism was dismissed as “Western bias” by pro-state voices.

The spread of fake news was defended by state-linked personalities as part of an “information war” or psyops campaign against Pakistan.

🔻Global Outcry Over Eroding Freedoms:

India dropped to 151st in Reporters Without Borders' Press Freedom Index.

The V-Dem Institute labeled India a leading autocratizing regime.

Watchdogs highlighted the increasing misuse of anti-terror laws, censorship, and harassment of independent media.

🔻Silent Retractions:

 After backlash, outlets like News18 and Zee News quietly edited or withdrew reports, admitting they couldn’t verify the information.

🔻The Bottom Line:
Critics warn that this is less about national security and more about controlling the public narrative. As censorship tightens and propaganda spreads, the foundations of free speech in the world’s largest democracy are visibly under threat.

PUBLIC STATEMENT BY PARANJOY GUHA THAKURTA
On the arbitrary takedown of https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe by Hostinger following legal notices from Indiabulls founder Sameer Gehlaut
October 31, 2026
On the morning of October 28, 2026, my website https://t.co/OeAAoTPXCy and all its associated subdomains, including https://t.co/I8kylhDXVk and https://t.co/D8b6LtNzWD, were abruptly taken offline by our web hosting provider, Hostinger (HOSTINGER operations, UAB). The website, registered twelve years ago, serves as an online archive of my work over several decades as a journalist, author, publisher, and maker of documentary films and music videos
Hostinger gave no prior intimation, warning, or opportunity to respond before suspending the entire hosting account. When my colleague contacted Hostinger “Support” at 6:48 AM on October 28, a hosting “specialist” stated that the suspension was triggered by an abuse report for "Fraud/Scam" and declared that "unsuspension is not negotiable in this case."
This sudden shutdown of an entire repository under the label "Fraud/Scam" happened just days after Sameer Gehlaut, founder of the Indiabulls group, served me with an ex parte court order demanding the removal of a single article published more than seven years on https://t.co/25noyNupwJ.
For over six years, Indiabulls and Shri Gehlaut have pursued legal action over this report and I have consistently defended our journalistic report in court. Here is the timeline:
·  March 11, 2020: Indiabulls Housing Finance Limited filed a criminal defamation complaint (CC No. 1765/2020) before the Patiala House Courts, New Delhi, against NewsClick, its Reader's Editor Urmilesh, co-author of the article Sourodipto Sanyal, NewsClick editor Prabir Purkayastha, and me over an article published on the website on September 30, 2019.
·  June 6, 2025 and July 9, 2025: More than five years after the complaint was filed, a Judicial Magistrate at Patiala House Courts passed an order on June 6, 2025, dropping proceedings against Shri Purkayastha while issuing summons to the remaining four accused, including me, under Sections 499 and 500 of the Indian Penal Code. A formal summons was issued on July 9, 2025, for appearance on July 30, 2025.
·  August 27, 2026: Counsel for Shri Gehlaut, sent me a legal notice demanding the takedown of the article within 24 to 48 hours, claiming that a status report by the Economic Offences Wing (EOW) of the Delhi Police had altered the factual position.
·  September 2, 2026: My counsel sent a reply pointing out concerns with the legal notice
·  October 24, 2026: Indiabulls Nests Limited (Plaintiff No. 1) and Sameer Gehlaut (Plaintiff No. 2) obtained an ex parte ad interim injunction from the Court of one of the District and Sessions Judges, Patiala House Courts, New Delhi, in Civil Suit No. 529/2026 (Indiabulls Nests Ltd. & Anr. v. Ashok Kumar/John Doe & Ors.), in which I am arrayed as Defendant No. 19. The order directed the removal and de-indexing of the article on https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe (listed as Item A-33 in Schedule A).
·  October 25, 2026 (10:13 AM IST): Advocates representing Indiabulls Nests Limited and Sameer Gehlaut, emailed me the October 24 court order and suit documents, demanding immediate deletion and written confirmation of compliance.
·  October 26, 2026 (11:33 PM IST): Sameer Gehlaut personally sent an email from his official address (sameer@indiabulls.com) demanding the immediate deletion of the URL from https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe and threatening to move the court under Order XXXIX Rule 2A of the Code of Civil Procedure if I did not comply, noting that the matter is next listed on December 18, 2026. While I was in the process of challenging the order dated 24.10.2026 before higher forums, on the same day, advocates representing Shri Gehlaut submitted a court order takedown complaint to Google LLC.

·  October 28, 2026 (3:16 PM IST): Google Search Console sent an automated notice ([WNC-598900]) informing me that Google was blocking the specific URL https://t.co/SsSVUVLKGX  from appearing in search results on https://t.co/2IOZ4I1WqC.

The Lumen Database record of this complaint (Notice ID: 101001876) reveals the scale of the takedown request. The complaint targeted 52 URLs on websites across major national and international news organisations, including The Economic Times, Business Standard, The Caravan, The Daily Pioneer, Business Today, Deccan Herald, ET Now, Financial Express, Livemint, Moneycontrol, Moneylife, NDTV Profit, The New Indian Express, Outlook Business, The Quint, Quartz, and NewsClick, along with posts on X (formerly Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, and Scribd.

Most of these reports on major corporate news websites remain accessible online. In fact, Item 39 on the Lumen takedown list is the original September 30, 2019 article published on https://t.co/qQP2N2fxA2: https://t.co/hgneAPvDuF, which remains live and accessible  as of now.

Yet, in the case of https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe, the entire domain and every website hosted on my account were wiped off the internet.

Hostinger's Baseless "Fraud/Scam" Claim and Demand for Accountability

Hostinger did not cite the Patiala House Courts order when it suspended my account on October 28, 2026. Instead, its representative claimed that the hosting account was permanently suspended due to an abuse report for "Fraud/Scam".

This allegation is demonstrably false:

1. VirusTotal Security Analysis: Independent domain checks conducted on October 28, 2026, at 7:48 AM and 7:54 AM on VirusTotal confirm that 0 out of 92 security vendors flagged https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe or https://t.co/I8kylhDXVk as malicious, phishing, or fraudulent. VirusTotal explicitly categorises https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe under "news and media".

2. Google Safe Browsing Status: Checks on the Google Safe Browsing diagnostic tool at 7:55 AM and 7:56 AM on October 28, 2026, for both https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe and https://t.co/D8b6LtNzWD returned the status: "No unsafe content found".
My website https://t.co/OeAAoTPXCy does not sell financial products, solicit funds for commercial schemes, or engage in any activity that could remotely be classified as a scam. It is a repository of public-interest journalism, books, documentary films, and investigative reports built over a lifetime of work. By acting on a fabricated "Fraud/Scam" abuse report without a single verification check or prior notice to the domain owner, Hostinger has allowed its abuse-reporting mechanism to be weaponised to censor an independent journalist.
Even where a court order directs the removal or de-indexing of a specific URL, a web hosting provider has no legal or ethical justification to pull down an entire domain and hundreds of unrelated articles, archives, and subdomains without notice.
I demand immediate answers and accountability from Hostinger:
1. Who submitted the false "Fraud/Scam" abuse report against https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe, and on what exact date and time was it received?
2. What internal verification did Hostinger's abuse team conduct before classifying a 12-year-old journalism portal as a "Fraud/Scam" site, especially when 92 security vendors on VirusTotal and Google Safe Browsing show zero malicious or unsafe content?
3. Why was no prior notice, warning, or copy of the complaint sent to me before suspending the entire hosting account?
4. On what basis did Hostinger's specialist declare that the suspension of an entire archive of journalistic work is "not negotiable"?
While my legal advisers are in the process of taking appropriate steps in court regarding the ex parte order dated October 24, 2026, and the wholesale suspension of my website, this backdoor censorship through web hosting providers sets a dangerous precedent for the independence of the media and freedom of expression as enshrined in Article (19)(1)(a) of the Constitution of India as a fundamental right of every citizen of India.
Yours sincerely

Paranjoy Guha Thakurta
Independent Journalist, Author, Publisher and Maker of Documentary Films and Music Videos

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

Amnesty International India stands in solidarity with the Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF), Software Freedom Law Center (SFLC) and geoblockedindia, whose work documenting internet censorship and defending digital rights is now being targeted through police notices seeking the removal of their social media accounts and posts.  The attempt to silence organizations and social media accounts for documenting censorship is deeply alarming. It threatens not only their freedom of expression but also the public's right to know when, why and how access to information is being restricted.  Those who expose censorship must not become its targets.

Under the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, social media companies have a responsibility to respect human rights, including the right to freedom of expression. They must carefully scrutinize government takedown requests, assess them against international human rights law, provide transparency, and challenge requests that are inconsistent with their human rights responsibilities.  Complying with demands to remove accounts and public-interest documentation without meaningful scrutiny risks enabling unlawful censorship and denying people access to information.  We urge @XCorpIndia to uphold its human rights obligations and protect the voices documenting restrictions on digital freedoms.

text:
Delhi Police asks X to take down IFF's account and posts. IFF will challenge the notices in court unless they are withdrawn.

The Delhi Police has asked X to remove the Internet Freedom Foundation's account, six of its posts, the accounts of SFLC and @geoblockedindia, and posts by 16 other users, on the ground that they defame the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh. The posts document and comment on a legal notice sent in the RSS's name to IFF, SFLC and @geoblockedindia, which demanded that the three stop criticising and documenting government blocking orders. IFF received copies of the two police notices from X on the morning of 3 November 2026.
IFF calls on the Delhi Police to withdraw both notices. If they are not withdrawn, IFF will challenge them in court.

What has happened

On 29 October 2026 at 9:54 PM, IFF, SFLC and the operator of @geoblockedindia received a two-page "legal notice" said to be issued on behalf of the RSS. It asked the three to stop opposing the government's blocking directions, stop documenting restricted content, stop posting details of geo-blocked posts, and confirm in writing within seven days that they would comply. It was signed by an unnamed "Authorised Signatory". Several RSS office-bearers have since said on X that the notice is not authentic. IFF replied to the notice, wrote to the RSS at its official address asking whether it had authorised it, and published both the notice and its reply on 30 October.

On 31 October 2026 at 8:06 PM, the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), Delhi Police, filed an "Illegal Content Report" with X (reference LD-321926). It listed two posts: IFF's post of 30 October on the notice, and SFLC post of the same day. The stated reason was that the posts are "defamatory towards the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023". The boxes for "safety/security", "defamation" and "other" were ticked. The fields for the nature of the court order and court order details were left empty. The desired action was "Remove/withhold content".

On 1 November 2026, a second notice arrived in the RSS's name. It said the matter had been handed to the Akhil Bharatiya Adhivakta Parishad, that complaints had been filed in several states, and that requests had been made to block IFF's X account and suspend the organisations. The Delhi Police had made its first request to X the previous evening. IFF did not know this until X told it on 3 November.

On 2 November 2026 at 8:51 AM, the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) filed a second notice with X (reference LD-322956). It lists 40 URLs. Thirty-seven are posts. Three are the entire accounts of @internetfreedom, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia. This time the boxes for "Hate speech", "defamation", "safety/security", "enforcement of court order" and "other" were all ticked. The court order fields were again left empty. The stated reason reads: "The posts constitute defamation and illegal content under Section 356 BNS. Under Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, read with Section 79(3)(b) IT Act, lawful notices require action within 3 hours."

The 16 other users are @ProdctiveUseful, @PanjwaniManoj, @jidge_, @RatanSharda55, @baxiabhishek, @SchrdingersDbag, @ashleshbiradar, @seemay, @NasirHussainINC, @Being_creat_ive, @AjoyDharmavaram, @othlaw, @_ananyaaa, @AimPoojaind, @incorigibleBhai and @rraoind. Their posts, as far as IFF can tell, comment on the notice or on the notice about it.

X forwarded both notice to IFF on 3 November 2026, at 8:47 AM and 10:03 AM, saying it was doing so "in the interest of transparency" and that IFF may wish to seek legal counsel and challenge the request in court. X's emails do not say that it has acted on the requests. The Delhi Police has not written to IFF, and no court has been approached, as far as the reports disclose. SFLC and @geoblockedindia have separately reported notifications from X about requests from the Uttar Pradesh Police, the Telangana Police and the Delhi Police's Cyber Crime unit, one of them against the whole of the @geoblockedindia account.

IFF's position

IFF condemns this legal action. A police force has made itself the enforcement arm of a private legal notice whose authenticity the organisation it names has not confirmed, and whose demand was that three organisations stop documenting censorship. The notices would deliver exactly what the notice asked for as they would also remove the accounts of the three groups in India that keep public records of what is blocked, and of who ordered it.

The posts in question are about a legal notice sent to us. They quote it, criticise how it was drafted, and say that we will carry on with our work. A person who receives a threat is entitled to publish it and answer it and that is not defamation of the sender. 

In the three weeks before the first notice, IFF assisted 86 people whose accounts were suspended or whose posts were withheld in India. SFLC's Free Speech Tracker recorded about 268 content restrictions and 83 account restrictions in the first 29 days of October. @geoblockedindia publishes the orders behind such blocks when platforms disclose them. None of this is unlawful. Documenting censorship and challenging it in court is what the Constitution expects of citizens.
IFF will not delete the posts. If the Delhi Police does not withdraw the notices, we will challenge them in court.

Why the reports are unlawful

Defamation is not a police matter. Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is a non-cognizable and bailable offence. Under Section 222 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, no court can take cognizance of it except on a complaint by the person aggrieved. 

Under Section 174 of the BNSS, the police cannot investigate a non-cognizable offence without an order of a Magistrate. The Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) is not the person aggrieved. The notices disclose no complaint by the RSS and no order of any Magistrate. Whether a statement is defamatory is for a court to decide after hearing its author, with the defences of truth, fair comment and good faith available to that author. 

In Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India, (2016) 7 SCC 221, the Supreme Court upheld criminal defamation on the strength of these safeguards. A police officer who asks a platform to remove speech as defamatory has decided the question himself, without a complainant, a court or a hearing.

The posts are protected comment. Exceptions 1 to 3 to Section 356(1) protect the truth published for the public good, opinion on the public conduct of public servants, and opinion on the conduct of any person touching a public question. The posts publish a notice that was sent to us and give our opinion of it. The RSS, if it sent the notice, chose to enter a public question. If it did not, the posts defame no one.

Further, Section 79(3)(b) and Rule 3(1)(d) do not permit this. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down Section 79(3)(b) so that an intermediary acquires "actual knowledge" only through a court order, or a notification from the appropriate government or its agency that unlawful acts relatable to Article 19(2) are being committed. The court said that it would be difficult for intermediaries to judge the legitimacy of the millions of requests they receive, and that the burden must not be placed on them. Rule 3(1)(d), as amended in November 2025 and February 2026, now requires the intimation to come from an officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary or Deputy Inspector General, to be reasoned, and to specify the legal basis and the nature of the unlawful act, subject to a monthly review by a Secretary-level officer. The three-hour window the notice invokes applies to a lawful order that meets these conditions. A web form that ticks "hate speech" and "enforcement of court order" while leaving the court order fields blank, and that gives one sentence of reasons for 40 URLs, is not such an order.

The notices by the Delhi Police are disproportionate. They seek to remove three accounts in their entirety, with years of posts, over six, four and eleven posts respectively. They sweep in 16 third parties whose only connection is that they commented on a public controversy. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that any restriction on speech must be necessary, proportionate and the least restrictive measure available, and that orders restricting speech must be published and reasoned. Removing an organisation's entire account for criticising a legal notice fails each of these tests.

The effect is to silence documentation of censorship and providing legal aid to Indian internet users. The accounts named are those that record blocking orders in India. The notice asked them to stop. A takedown request that accomplishes the demand of an anonymous private notice is not law enforcement. It is the use of state power for a private end, which Article 14 forbids.

Our demands

1. To the Delhi Police: Withdraw reports LD-321926 and LD-322956 and confirm the withdrawal in writing to X and to IFF. 

2. To the Delhi Police: Disclose the complaint on which the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) acted, the authority under which the reports were filed, and whether any order of a Magistrate under Section 174 BNSS exists. Disclose every request made to any platform in this matter, including those made by the Cyber Crime unit against @geoblockedindia.

3. To X: Do not act on the reports. If any content is withheld in India, tell the affected user before acting, give them the full request, and name the legal basis. Publish both reports to the Lumen database, as the reporting form itself contemplates.

4. To the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology and the Ministry of Home Affairs: Have the Secretary-level review required by Rule 3(1)(d) examine these intimations, and tell police forces that Rule 3(1)(d) is not a remedy for defamation, which the law reserves to the person aggrieved and to the courts.

5. To the RSS: State publicly whether it authorised either notice or any complaint to the police. If it did not, say so to the Delhi Police.

If the notices are not withdrawn, IFF will challenge them in court. We will continue to document blocking orders, to publish them, and to provide legal assistance to anyone whose account or post is withheld in India. Nothing in these notices changes that.

text:
X tells Delhi High Court that the notices attributed to Delhi Police were sent by an imposter.

On 29 October 2026, Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) and Software Freedom Law Centre (SFLC), received a legal notice from an individual identifying themselves as Advocate Gaurav Tiwari, claiming to be acting on behalf of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS).

The notice demanded that they stop documenting government content restrictions, opposing blocking directions and publishing details of geo-blocked content in India. It also asked for written confirmation within seven days that we would comply.

A second notice followed on 1 November, referring to the Akhil Bharatiya Adhivakta Parishad (ABAP), complaints in different states and requests to block their social media accounts.

On 3 November, X forwarded takedown requests purportedly submitted by the Delhi Police. These included requests targeting the accounts of IFF, SFLC and GeoBlockedIndia, along with several individual posts and posts by other users.
The requests cited alleged defamation under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), among other grounds.

However, questions about the authenticity of these requests continued. SFLC attempted to verify them with the Delhi Police, but its communications to the email address mentioned in the notices were returned as undeliverable. The organisations also approached the Delhi Police for clarification.

On 5 November, IFF and SFLC approached the Delhi High Court challenging the notices.

On 6 November, X told the Delhi High Court that the notices attributed to Delhi Police were sent by an imposter, not the Delhi Police.

X informed the Court that it had conducted an internal investigation, found that the notices were sent by an imposter, and filed a complaint with Delhi Police.

X also confirmed that the accounts of IFF and SFLC would not be taken down. Following this submission, the Delhi High Court disposed of their petitions.

Separately, a Scroll investigation found that the original legal notices sent in the name of the RSS were also part of an apparent hoax. The investigation traced the address and phone number mentioned in those notices to another organisation, Rashtriya Seva Sangh, whose president denied sending them.

The two developments now establish that both the original notices sent in the RSS's name and the subsequent takedown requests attributed to Delhi Police were not authentic.

I have my twitter back. 

It took me 6 days, a cyber police complaint and a legal notice to twitter to recover my account. 

If you got a DM from me last week asking you to vote for me for a podcast, that was not me. Please don't click it & If you already did, please change your password ASAP.

Here's what happened:

→I received a late night DM from a friend to vote on a podcast which redirected me to a a login page that looked right, and I typed in my password (classic)

→The attacker logged in and changed my 2FA within minutes & I was locked out of my account. (I still don't understand how my email and phone number were changed. Neither my email nor my phone was compromised.)

→Then he used account to DM followers a fake "vote for me" link. Each person who clicks becomes the next account sending it. That is how these spread.

What didn't work:

→ I filed X's hacked account form within the hour. Less than two hours later, the reply came: X could not verify me as the account owner. Their suggestion was to create a new account. Once 2FA is changed, the automated system treats the attacker as the real owner.

→ So I went to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, 2021, X must appoint a Resident Grievance Officer in India. He has no email address. X does not accept legal notices by email. 

The only options are a web form or post to their physical office.

Here's what worked:

→First, a cyber complaint on https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW (or call 1930).

→Second, a legal notice to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, impersonation complaints must be acted on within 24 hours.

→Third, the same notice sent by registered post, and to every X email address I could find.

The notice put X on record. It set out the ticket number, the phishing link, and the cyber complaint number. It showed proof of ownership: the registered email, the phone number, and the Premium subscription paid from my card. It ended with a clear ask and a deadline.

Six days after the hack, I was back in.

If this happens to you:
• Act within hours
• File X's hacked account form from your registered email and be persistent (this is important)
• File at https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW and keep the acknowledgement
• Notice to the Grievance Officer via the https://t.co/YkDfcMQwzE form and by post
